title: The hymn that quotes its doubters
hookLine: "where is he?" some ask. "he is not," some say. a hymn to Indra quotes its doubters out loud
carry: shraddha: trust you place, even beside doubt

lines: A HYMN THAT QUOTES ITS DOUBTERS.
cards: "Where is he?" people ask. "He isn't real," others answer. It could be an argument at a dinner table this week.

It's a line from a hymn in the Rig Veda, book two, and the god being doubted is Indra: the storm, the warrior, the one who breaks the dam and lets the rivers run. The hymn could have left the doubters out.
Instead it quotes them, right in the middle of the praise. Today: the second voice, Indra.

teach.b: Indra is the mighty one of the Rig Veda's storms. In its stories he fights Vritra, a serpent coiled around the waters, and when Indra strikes him down, the rivers pour free.

Book two, hymn twelve, praises him in a shape you can hear even in paraphrase. Verse after verse tells something he did: he steadied the shaking earth, spread out the sky, killed the serpent and set the rivers flowing.
And verse after verse ends the same way. Sa janasa indrah. He, O people, is Indra.
Then, in the fifth verse, the hymn turns.
In paraphrase: the terrible one, about whom they ask, where is he? About whom they say, he is not. The singer's answer isn't an argument.
It's shrad asmai dhatta: put your trust in him. Listen to those two phrases, because Hindu tradition still uses them.
He is not has na asti in it: is not. The same two words later give Sanskrit its word nastika, one who says, there is not.

teach.h: SHRAD DHATTA → SHRADDHA: TRUST YOU PLACE.
teach.b: And put your trust holds the roots of shraddha: faith, trust you choose to place, which many scholars hear as setting your heart on something. Here's the teaching. The Veda doesn't hide doubt.
It names the doubter in his own words, and answers with shraddha, not proof. Centuries later the Gita says a person is made of their shraddha: as your trust is, so are you.

how: Hymns to Indra are part of the Rig Veda's recitation, kept in Vedic schools; in later Hindu stories Indra appears as king of the gods and lord of rain.

o: praise songs that quote the doubters, then answer with trust
spells recited to stop a storm from breaking
debates written to prove a god is real

p: one who says, there is not

s: the hymn to Indra leaves out anyone who doubts him
its fifth verse quotes them: where is he? he is not.
the hymn answers its doubters with a proof
it answers with shraddha: put your trust in him. he, O people, is Indra.
the word shraddha shares its roots with the hymn's "put your trust in him"
shrad and dha: to place trust. the Gita later says a person is made of their shraddha.

games.q: you're singing Indra's praise, and you know some people say he isn't there. what does the hymn do?
o: leave them out of the hymn
quote them, then answer: put your trust in him
games.why: the hymn quotes them, where is he? he is not, and answers with shraddha, not proof: put your trust in him.

practice: Let one honest doubt be asked, about God, or whether any of this is true, without arguing it away.
Then do what the hymn does: place your trust somewhere, even something small: a name of God you grew up with, the people who taught you, the breath coming back.
If you pray, say that name once, slowly, and let the doubt sit beside it. If you don't, simply notice where your trust already rests.

wordCard.voice: Hymns to Agni, and today, to Indra. In Rig Veda two, twelve, each verse ends, he, O people, is Indra; one verse quotes those who say, he is not, and answers, put your trust in him. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Indra, the Rig Veda's storm and warrior god, who frees the waters from Vritra.

carryVoice: Your line: shraddha, trust you place, even beside doubt. The hymn kept the doubter's words and still sang. Go gently.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 2.12 (the refrain; verse 2 the earth steadied and the sky spread; verse 3 the serpent killed and the rivers freed; verse 5 the doubters and the call to trust)
Rig Veda 1.32 (Indra and Vritra; the waters released)
Bhagavad Gita 17.3 (a person is made of their shraddha; as one's shraddha is, so is one)
